reasoning: The trap is real: GeminiWireTypes.swift:150 reads `rem` with no clamp, and :154 does Int((rem*100).rounded()), which traps on huge values like 1e300 and on NaN. But no attacker who crosses a trust boundary controls either input. (1) The HTTP path only reaches generativelanguage.googleapis.com over https. GeminiConfig.validate (AppConfig.swift:557-569) enforces https, a single-host allowlist (AppConfig.swift:512-514) and the API-version path, and the provider builds the request from that validated baseURL (GeminiProvider.swift:45,89). Forging the body therefore takes Google itself or a TLS MITM with a trusted CA. That is an upstream compromise, not an attacker the app is exposed to. (2) The agy path runs a local executable. It comes from the user's own config agy_path or from fixed install locations (~/.local/bin, /opt/homebrew/bin, /usr/local/bin, ~/.gemini/antigravity/bin; AntigravityExecutor.swift:28-48). All of these are writable only by the user or an admin, and each is already a way to run code as the user. Anyone who can replace agy already has code execution as that user, far more than a crash. The only trusted author of real agy output is Google's own CLI. The finding's precondition, 'attacker controls the agy output or the Gemini API response', is therefore not reachable in the default deploy. What remains is a robustness bug (the unclamped Int conversion) with no attacker-controlled source.
